A strong argument that Donald Trump was an ineffective president—especially judging his first term by durable policy results, crisis management, and institutional leadership—would look like this:

1. **He struggled to turn campaign promises into lasting legislation.**  
   Trump entered office with Republican control of both houses of Congress, yet many of his biggest promises went unfulfilled. He did not repeal and replace the Affordable Care Act, did not build a Mexico-funded border wall, did not pass a major bipartisan infrastructure package, and did not substantially reduce the national debt. His signature legislative achievement, the 2017 tax law, passed, but it did not accomplish his stated goal of eliminating deficits or delivering broadly shared long-term gains.

2. **His administration was marked by unusually high turnover and internal disorder.**  
   Effective presidents build stable teams and coordinate agencies toward clear goals. Trump’s first administration saw frequent departures and firings among chiefs of staff, national-security advisers, cabinet officials, and senior aides. Public infighting, contradictory messages, and policy reversals made it harder for agencies, allies, businesses, and the public to know what the government’s position was.

3. **His COVID-19 response exposed serious weaknesses in crisis leadership.**  
   The pandemic was the defining crisis of Trump’s first term. While his administration helped accelerate vaccine development through Operation Warp Speed, Trump repeatedly downplayed the virus, clashed with public-health officials, promoted unproven treatments, and gave inconsistent guidance on masks, testing, and reopening. The United States experienced very high death totals and severe economic disruption. A president’s effectiveness is tested in emergencies, and Trump’s communication and coordination failures weakened public trust at a critical time.

4. **He governed heavily through executive action rather than durable consensus.**  
   Trump often relied on executive orders, emergency declarations, and administrative changes—such as using emergency powers to redirect funds toward border barriers. Such moves can produce short-term results, but they are vulnerable to court challenges and reversal by later administrations. Effective governance usually requires building enough legislative and public support that policies endure beyond one presidency.

5. **His foreign policy created uncertainty without consistently producing clear gains.**  
   Trump was right that allies should contribute more to collective defense and that China posed serious economic and strategic challenges. But his confrontational approach toward NATO allies, withdrawal from agreements, and unpredictable trade policy often created uncertainty. His tariffs on China led to retaliatory tariffs that hurt many American farmers and required large federal aid payments. The result was not a clear, durable resolution of the trade imbalance or of China’s economic practices.

6. **He increased polarization instead of building coalitions.**  
   Presidents are more effective when they can persuade people beyond their core supporters. Trump’s rhetoric often attacked opponents, media organizations, civil servants, judges, and even members of his own party. That approach energized his base but made compromise and sustained governing harder. It also contributed to a political climate in which even useful policies became more difficult to implement because trust was so low.

7. **His conduct after the 2020 election damaged democratic institutions.**  
   Trump’s refusal to accept the election result, his unsupported claims of widespread fraud, and his pressure campaign against officials undermined confidence in elections. The January 6 attack on the Capitol was the most severe consequence. Whatever one thinks of his policy agenda, a president who weakens public trust in peaceful transfers of power is failing a central responsibility of the office.

8. **Even his economic record was mixed and incomplete.**  
   Supporters point to low unemployment and rising markets before COVID-19. But those trends largely continued an expansion that began before he took office, while deficits rose substantially even before the pandemic. A president cannot be judged only by favorable conditions during part of a term; fiscal discipline, resilience, and the ability to manage downturns matter too.

A fair conclusion is not that Trump achieved nothing. He appointed conservative judges, enacted tax cuts, signed criminal-justice reform, pursued deregulation, and helped speed vaccine development. But effectiveness is more than producing a list of actions. It means converting goals into durable results, managing crises competently, maintaining capable institutions, and protecting democratic stability. By those measures, Trump’s first presidency can be argued to have been ineffective and unusually damaging.

A case that Donald Trump is an effective president can be made by focusing on his ability to translate campaign promises into concrete policy changes, reshape institutions, and dominate the political agenda.

1. **He delivers visible policy outcomes.**  
   Trump’s first term produced major actions aligned with his campaign platform: the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, deregulation across energy and business sectors, tougher immigration enforcement, renegotiation of NAFTA into the USMCA, and a more confrontational trade policy toward China. Whether one agrees with each policy or not, they demonstrate a president willing and able to act on stated priorities.

2. **He has had a lasting impact on the federal judiciary.**  
   Trump appointed three Supreme Court justices—Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh, and Amy Coney Barrett—as well as a large number of lower-court judges. Those appointments have shifted the judiciary for decades, affecting issues including abortion, administrative power, gun rights, and religious liberty. Few presidential achievements are as durable as shaping the courts.

3. **He is unusually effective at setting the agenda.**  
   Trump forces both allies and opponents to respond to his priorities, especially on immigration, trade, border security, crime, and skepticism of international institutions. Even politicians who criticize him have often adopted tougher rhetoric or policies in response to the issues he elevated. Agenda-setting is a central measure of political effectiveness.

4. **He challenges established assumptions in foreign policy.**  
   Supporters point to the Abraham Accords, which normalized relations between Israel and several Arab states, as an important diplomatic achievement. They also credit him with pressing NATO allies to increase defense spending and with pursuing a more transactional foreign policy intended to prioritize U.S. interests.

5. **He appeals directly to voters who felt ignored.**  
   Trump’s political strength comes from his ability to communicate with working-class and nontraditional Republican voters in direct, simple terms. He has built a durable coalition around concerns about economic globalization, immigration, cultural change, and distrust of political elites. An effective president must not only govern but maintain a political base capable of sustaining an agenda.

6. **He is willing to confront bureaucracy and entrenched institutions.**  
   Trump’s supporters see his conflict with federal agencies, the media, corporate leadership, and foreign-policy establishments as evidence that he is willing to challenge systems they believe are unaccountable. His critics call this disruptive; supporters call it necessary. Either way, he has proven capable of changing the terms of debate and forcing institutional resistance into the open.

The strongest version of the argument is not that Trump is universally popular or that every decision has succeeded. It is that effectiveness means accomplishing priorities, reshaping institutions, mobilizing supporters, and leaving a durable mark on policy—and by those measures, Trump has been an unusually consequential and effective president.

Joe Biden was an effective president because he governed in the face of extraordinary challenges and produced substantial, lasting results. He entered office amid a pandemic, an economic crisis, deep political division, and weakening confidence in democratic institutions. Rather than merely managing those problems, his administration enacted major legislation, invested in the country’s future, strengthened alliances, and helped guide the United States toward a more stable economic recovery.

One of Biden’s most immediate accomplishments was overseeing the nation’s recovery from COVID-19. When he took office in January 2021, vaccines were available but distribution was uneven, schools and businesses were struggling, and millions of Americans remained out of work. The American Rescue Plan provided direct assistance to families, expanded child tax credits, funded vaccination and public-health efforts, and helped state and local governments avoid severe budget cuts. Critics debated the size of the package, but its central purpose was clear: prevent a weak recovery from becoming a prolonged economic disaster. Employment rebounded rapidly, and the United States recovered jobs faster than many other advanced economies.

Biden also proved effective at translating broad campaign promises into legislation. The bipartisan Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act was one of the most important domestic laws passed in decades. It committed major investments to roads, bridges, public transit, airports, ports, broadband internet, clean water systems, and electric-vehicle charging. These are not glamorous achievements, but they are fundamental to economic competitiveness and daily life. For years, politicians of both parties had promised to rebuild American infrastructure. Biden succeeded in getting it done.

His economic agenda also addressed long-term industrial and environmental challenges. The CHIPS and Science Act invested in domestic semiconductor manufacturing and research, seeking to reduce American dependence on foreign supply chains for crucial technology. The COVID-19 pandemic had revealed how vulnerable the economy was to disruptions in global production. By encouraging semiconductor factories and high-tech investment in the United States, the Biden administration sought to create jobs while improving national security.

Similarly, the Inflation Reduction Act represented the most significant federal investment in clean energy and climate action in American history. It created incentives for renewable energy, electric vehicles, battery production, and energy-efficient homes. The law was not only an environmental measure; it was an industrial policy designed to ensure that the United States competes in the growing global clean-energy economy. Its impact will be measured over decades, but its direction is clear: Biden used federal policy to encourage domestic manufacturing and technological innovation rather than allowing the country to fall behind China and Europe.

Biden’s administration also made meaningful progress on health care. It allowed Medicare to negotiate prices for certain prescription drugs, capped insulin costs for many seniors, extended health-insurance subsidies, and took steps to reduce the cost of medications. These changes may seem incremental, but for Americans struggling to afford essential treatment, they are deeply consequential. Effective presidents do not only make grand speeches; they make practical improvements in people’s lives.

In foreign policy, Biden faced a world made more dangerous by Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. His administration helped organize an international coalition supporting Ukraine while avoiding a direct war between the United States and Russia. He worked with NATO allies to impose sanctions, provide military aid, and reinforce European security. Under Biden, NATO expanded to include Finland and Sweden, demonstrating that Russia’s aggression had strengthened rather than fractured the alliance. This was a significant diplomatic achievement.

Of course, Biden’s presidency had failures and controversies. The withdrawal from Afghanistan was chaotic and painful. Inflation became a serious burden for families, regardless of its multiple global causes. The border remained a difficult challenge, and political polarization did not disappear. An honest evaluation of his presidency must recognize these shortcomings.

But effectiveness does not mean perfection. It means achieving meaningful results under difficult conditions. Biden governed during a pandemic, global supply-chain disruption, war in Europe, and persistent partisan obstruction. Yet he passed landmark laws, created conditions for major investments in American industry, expanded health-care protections, strengthened alliances, and helped prevent an economic collapse from becoming a long-term crisis.

History may continue to debate every part of Joe Biden’s record. Still, the evidence shows that he was more than a caretaker president. He was an effective leader whose policies reshaped infrastructure, manufacturing, climate policy, health care, and America’s role in the world.

**The Case That Joe Biden Was an Ineffective President**

Presidential effectiveness should be judged not only by intentions or legislation passed, but by whether a president delivers stability, public confidence, competent administration, and durable solutions to the country’s most serious problems. By that standard, Joe Biden’s presidency was ineffective. Although his administration enacted several major laws, it struggled to translate those achievements into improved living conditions, political unity, or a sense that the federal government was in control of events.

The most damaging weakness of Biden’s presidency was the economy. Biden inherited an economy recovering from the COVID-19 pandemic, and employment eventually remained strong. But many Americans did not experience the recovery as a success because inflation severely eroded their purchasing power. Consumer-price inflation reached 9.1 percent in June 2022, the highest level in roughly four decades. Grocery bills, rent, fuel, and interest rates rose sharply, making ordinary life more expensive for working- and middle-class families.

Biden cannot fairly be blamed for every cause of inflation; supply-chain disruptions, global energy shocks, and the war in Ukraine all mattered. Nevertheless, his administration contributed to the problem by supporting the massive American Rescue Plan in 2021, even as some economists warned that additional stimulus could overheat the economy. More important, Biden repeatedly appeared slow to recognize the seriousness of inflation. A president does not control every economic force, but effective leadership requires acknowledging problems early and persuading the public that there is a credible plan to address them. Biden often failed to do so.

Biden’s handling of the southern border was another example of ineffective governance. The United States experienced historically high numbers of migrant encounters during his presidency, straining border communities, city budgets, immigration courts, and social-service systems. The issue was complicated: instability in Latin America, global migration patterns, and congressional inaction all played roles. Yet Biden’s administration sent mixed signals, reversed some Trump-era policies without immediately implementing workable alternatives, and spent years struggling to establish a consistent approach. By the time Biden embraced tougher enforcement measures and negotiated a bipartisan border proposal in 2024, public trust on immigration had already deteriorated.

Foreign policy also exposed Biden’s limitations. His decision to end the war in Afghanistan reflected a broadly popular desire to stop an endless conflict. However, the execution of the withdrawal was widely viewed as chaotic. Images of desperate civilians at Kabul’s airport, the collapse of the Afghan government, and the deaths of 13 U.S. service members in a suicide bombing created the impression of an administration unprepared for predictable consequences. Ending the war may have been defensible; the manner in which it was done was not. Effective presidents anticipate crises rather than react to them after the fact.

Biden also struggled to project a coherent strategy in major international conflicts. His support for Ukraine helped rally Western allies against Russia’s invasion, and that was a significant accomplishment. But the war became prolonged and costly, while U.S. support became increasingly politically divisive. In the Middle East, Biden faced criticism from multiple sides over the Israel-Hamas war: some believed he was too supportive of Israel’s military campaign, while others argued he pressured an important ally without achieving meaningful humanitarian or diplomatic progress. In both cases, Biden often appeared caught between competing goals rather than able to define and execute a clear strategy.

Supporters of Biden point to the bipartisan infrastructure law, the CHIPS and Science Act, and the Inflation Reduction Act as evidence of success. These were substantial legislative accomplishments, especially in a polarized era. But passing laws is only part of the job. The benefits of those measures were often slow to reach voters, poorly communicated, or overshadowed by immediate concerns about inflation, crime, immigration, and international instability. A president who cannot convince the public that his agenda is improving their lives has not fully succeeded as a political leader.

Ultimately, Biden’s presidency illustrates the difference between activity and effectiveness. His administration was active: it spent heavily, passed major bills, and intervened in domestic and foreign crises. Yet Americans were left with persistent economic anxiety, a deeply troubled border, declining confidence in national institutions, and a widespread sense that the country was moving in the wrong direction. Biden may have had admirable goals and real legislative achievements, but his inability to manage crises, communicate convincingly, and deliver visible results makes a strong case that he was an ineffective president.

Inflation reduced Americans’ confidence in the economy, border challenges created doubts about enforcement, the Afghanistan withdrawal raised questions about competence, and international crises exposed the limits of his diplomacy. Whether this judgment is ultimately fair remains debated, but the perception of ineffective leadership was a central weakness of Biden’s presidency.

Assessing a president fairly requires more than looking at a single news cycle or one economic statistic. It requires asking whether the president responded to major challenges, delivered meaningful legislation, strengthened the country’s long-term position, and governed competently in difficult circumstances. By those standards, Joe Biden was an effective president. His administration helped guide the United States out of the COVID-19 crisis, produced significant bipartisan legislation, invested in American infrastructure and manufacturing, expanded health-care protections, and reinforced U.S. alliances abroad.

Biden took office in January 2021 during an extraordinary period of instability. The country was still dealing with the COVID-19 pandemic, high unemployment, disrupted schools, and economic uncertainty. His administration oversaw a rapid vaccination campaign and signed the American Rescue Plan, which provided direct financial assistance, expanded the child tax credit, supported state and local governments, and helped schools reopen. While economists debate the law’s effects on inflation, there is little question that the recovery in jobs was strong. Unemployment fell to historically low levels during Biden’s presidency, and millions of Americans returned to work after the pandemic recession.

One of Biden’s clearest accomplishments was his ability to turn long-neglected policy goals into law. The bipartisan Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act committed major funding to repairing roads, bridges, ports, public transit, water systems, and broadband access. For decades, politicians in both parties promised an infrastructure package but failed to deliver one. Biden succeeded where many predecessors had not. These investments matter not only because they create jobs in the short term, but because they improve the nation’s economic competitiveness for years to come.

Biden also worked to restore American manufacturing and reduce dependence on foreign supply chains. The CHIPS and Science Act encouraged semiconductor production in the United States, responding to shortages that had affected everything from automobiles to consumer electronics. The law aimed to ensure that the United States remains competitive with China in advanced technology while creating skilled manufacturing jobs at home. At a time when both Democrats and Republicans agree that America must strengthen its industrial base, Biden translated that concern into concrete policy.

His climate and energy policies were another major achievement. The Inflation Reduction Act included the largest federal investment in clean energy in American history. It created incentives for electric vehicles, renewable power, battery production, energy-efficient homes, and domestic clean-energy manufacturing. These measures addressed climate change while also encouraging businesses to build factories and supply chains in the United States. Rather than treating environmental protection and economic growth as opposites, the administration tied them together through investment and job creation.

Biden also made important progress on health care. His administration allowed Medicare to begin negotiating prices for certain prescription drugs, a reform that presidents of both parties had struggled to achieve. It capped insulin costs for many Medicare beneficiaries at $35 per month and extended Affordable Care Act subsidies, helping more Americans afford health insurance. These policies directly improved the lives of seniors, working families, and people with chronic medical conditions.

In foreign policy, Biden faced the most serious challenge to European security in decades when Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022. His administration coordinated a broad international response, strengthened NATO cooperation, and helped rally democratic allies against Russian aggression. Finland joined NATO during his presidency, and Sweden’s accession process moved forward as well, expanding the alliance in response to Russia’s actions. While Americans can reasonably debate the scale and duration of U.S. aid to Ukraine, Biden’s ability to unite allies showed effective international leadership.

Of course, Biden’s presidency was not without weaknesses. Inflation rose sharply after the pandemic, placing real strain on household budgets. The administration also faced persistent criticism over immigration and the southern border. The withdrawal from Afghanistan was chaotic and painful. These are serious issues, and acknowledging them is necessary for an honest assessment. Yet effective presidents are not those who avoid every crisis; they are those who make consequential progress despite them.

Biden governed during a period shaped by a pandemic, global supply disruptions, war in Europe, political polarization, and rising competition with China. In that difficult environment, he passed landmark laws, oversaw a strong employment recovery, strengthened infrastructure, promoted domestic industry, expanded health-care affordability, and rebuilt key alliances. Whatever one thinks of every decision he made, the record shows that Joe Biden was an effective president because he turned major national challenges into lasting policy achievements.

**Why Joe Biden Was an Ineffective President**

A president’s effectiveness should be measured not simply by intentions or isolated legislative victories, but by whether the country becomes safer, more prosperous, more united, and more confident in its future. By that standard, Joe Biden’s presidency was ineffective. Although his administration passed major spending bills and promoted ambitious domestic goals, it repeatedly struggled to manage inflation, border security, foreign-policy crises, public confidence, and political division. Biden’s presidency illustrates the difference between passing legislation and governing successfully.

The most immediate failure of the Biden years was the cost of living. When Biden entered office in 2021, Americans were emerging from the economic disruptions of the COVID-19 pandemic. His administration responded with the $1.9 trillion American Rescue Plan, which included worthwhile support for families and communities. But critics argued that adding such a large stimulus package to an economy already recovering contributed to overheating demand and worsening inflation. Inflation eventually reached its highest levels in roughly four decades, peaking above 9 percent in 2022. Families saw grocery bills, rents, electricity costs, and interest rates rise sharply.

The White House often blamed inflation on global supply-chain problems, Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, and corporate pricing practices. Those factors did matter. Yet effective leadership requires recognizing when one’s own policies are adding to a problem and adjusting quickly. Instead, the administration was slow to acknowledge the seriousness and persistence of inflation. For many Americans, the technical debates in Washington mattered less than the simple reality that their paychecks did not stretch as far as before. An economy can look strong in statistical reports while still feeling unaffordable to working families, and Biden failed to close that gap between official optimism and daily experience.

Biden was also ineffective on the southern border. During his presidency, the United States experienced historically high levels of migrant encounters at the U.S.-Mexico border. Immigration is a complicated issue involving economic hardship, political instability, criminal networks, and asylum law. Still, the federal government’s core responsibility is to maintain an orderly and credible immigration system. Biden’s administration often appeared reactive rather than prepared, alternating between softer rhetoric, legal restrictions, executive actions, and negotiations that came only after the situation had become a major national political crisis.

The administration did eventually support a bipartisan border-security proposal in 2024, but by then public trust had already eroded. A more effective president would have treated border management as an urgent responsibility from the beginning rather than allowing it to become a symbol of governmental dysfunction. The result was frustration across the political spectrum: conservatives believed the administration failed to enforce immigration laws, while many progressives were disappointed by the later adoption of stricter measures.

Foreign policy exposed another major weakness: Biden’s handling of the withdrawal from Afghanistan. Ending the long war was not necessarily a mistake; many Americans across party lines supported bringing U.S. troops home. The failure was in the execution. The rapid collapse of the Afghan government, the chaos at Kabul’s airport, and the deaths of 13 American service members during an ISIS-K attack created an image of disorder and poor planning. Thousands of Afghans who had assisted American forces were left in danger, while Americans watched desperate scenes unfold from the airport.

The Afghanistan withdrawal damaged American credibility abroad. Allies questioned whether the United States would manage future commitments responsibly, while adversaries saw an opportunity to test American resolve. Biden later demonstrated leadership by rallying NATO support for Ukraine after Russia’s 2022 invasion, an achievement his supporters rightly emphasize. But strong support for Ukraine does not erase the fact that Afghanistan represented one of the most visible and consequential failures of presidential leadership in recent years.

Biden also struggled to unite the country. He entered office promising to restore normalcy and reduce political hostility after the Trump years. Instead, the country remained deeply divided, and public trust in major institutions continued to decline. Not all of this polarization was Biden’s fault; American political conflict had been escalating for years. Still, presidents are judged partly by their ability to communicate clearly, reassure the public, and build durable coalitions. Biden often seemed unable to make a compelling case for his agenda in language that connected with voters outside his party’s base.

His administration achieved significant policy goals, including the bipartisan infrastructure law, investments in semiconductor manufacturing, and clean-energy incentives through the Inflation Reduction Act. These accomplishments should not be ignored. However, they did not overcome the broader perception that the administration was out of touch with ordinary concerns. Voters cared about affordable housing, food prices, public safety, immigration, and uncertainty abroad. Biden’s team frequently emphasized long-term investments and positive economic indicators, while many Americans felt their immediate problems were being dismissed.

Finally, Biden’s age and apparent limitations became an unavoidable issue. The concern was not merely that he was older than previous presidents. It was that many voters repeatedly questioned whether he had the energy, clarity, and stamina required for one of the world’s most demanding jobs. His public appearances, verbal missteps, and uneven performances reinforced worries that his administration was being managed by aides rather than led decisively by the president himself. Whether fair or not, leadership depends heavily on public confidence. Biden did not inspire enough of it.

Joe Biden’s presidency was not without accomplishments, and a fair assessment should acknowledge them. But presidents are ultimately judged by results. During Biden’s term, Americans faced high inflation, an uncontrolled border crisis, a chaotic withdrawal from Afghanistan, continued political division, and declining confidence in national leadership. His administration often had explanations for these failures, but explanations are not the same as solutions. Biden may have pursued well-intentioned policies, yet his presidency showed that good intentions and large spending programs cannot substitute for decisive, competent, and effective leadership.

## Evidence supporting the claim

### 1. Democracy and rule of law
Democrats generally place strong emphasis on voting access, independent elections, protections against political violence, and acceptance of election results. Polling consistently finds broad public support for measures such as secure elections, peaceful transfers of power, and protecting democratic institutions.

Democrats tend to support civil-rights protections for racial minorities, women, LGBTQ people, religious minorities, immigrants, and people with disabilities. Equality before the law is a foundational American principle, rooted in the Declaration of Independence and the Fourteenth Amendment.

Majorities often support many of these positions in broad terms—for example, legal same-sex marriage and protections against employment discrimination.

This case rests on an American tradition as old as the New Deal: freedom requires more than the absence of government interference; it also requires a realistic ability to participate in society and advance economically.

Critics argue that Democratic policies can expand government, raise costs, discourage work or investment, and create dependency. The United States has no single agreed civic ideology: Americans value liberty and limited government, but also equality, democracy, pluralism, opportunity, religious freedom, security, and compassion. ## Evidence supporting the claim

**1. Limited government, self-reliance, and free enterprise**  
Republicans traditionally emphasize lower taxes, deregulation, private business, property rights, and skepticism of federal power. Those positions connect to longstanding American ideals of individual initiative and economic freedom. Many Americans—especially conservatives, business owners, and rural voters—see government overreach as a major threat to liberty.

**2. Patriotism, national cohesion, and public safety**  
The party often places strong emphasis on national symbols, military strength, border enforcement, law enforcement, and a common national identity. These resonate with Americans who view sovereignty, order, and civic loyalty as essential to the country’s character.

**3. Religious liberty and socially conservative values**  
Republicans are more likely to defend public expressions of religion, parental authority, traditional family norms, and restrictions on abortion. Since religion remains important to many Americans, particularly Christians, this can be seen as representing an influential strand of American culture.

**4. Electoral support demonstrates real representation**  
Republicans regularly win large shares of the vote and control many state governments, especially in rural and Southern states. Their continued electoral success is evidence that their values reflect the beliefs of a substantial portion of Americans—not merely a fringe.

**5. Skepticism of elite institutions**  
Many Republican voters believe media organizations, universities, federal agencies, and large corporations are disconnected from ordinary people. The party’s anti-establishment language can appeal to an American tradition of distrust toward concentrated power.

## Evidence against the claim

**1. American values also include equality and pluralism**  
The country is racially, religiously, and culturally diverse, and many Americans place high value on civil rights, inclusion, and equal treatment. Republican positions on immigration, voting rules, LGBTQ rights, affirmative action, and abortion are viewed by critics as insufficiently responsive to those values, especially by younger voters and many minority communities.

**2. Democratic norms and the peaceful transfer of power**  
A central American value is constitutional democracy: free elections, rule of law, and peaceful acceptance of electoral results. Republican efforts to challenge the 2020 election, the role of some party figures in promoting unsupported fraud claims, and the January 6 attack on the Capitol significantly weaken the argument that the party consistently represents democratic civic values. Not all Republicans supported those actions, and some strongly opposed them, but the party’s internal response has been uneven.

**3. “Limited government” is applied inconsistently**  
Critics argue that Republicans favor limited government mainly in economic regulation and taxation, while supporting expansive state power in other areas—such as abortion restrictions, immigration enforcement, classroom-content laws, or limits on certain corporate and local-government policies. This does not necessarily make those policies illegitimate, but it complicates a simple claim to be the party of personal freedom.

**4. Majority opinion often differs by issue**  
On several issues, national polling has often found majority support for positions more associated with Democrats: protecting abortion access in at least some circumstances, stronger environmental action, legal recognition of same-sex marriage, and expanded health-care access. If “representing American values” means matching majority public opinion issue by issue, Republicans do not consistently have the stronger claim.

**5. Economic opportunity is contested**  
Republicans argue that tax cuts and market freedom create opportunity. Opponents argue that these policies can widen inequality, weaken worker protections, and reduce access to education, health care, and social mobility. Americans broadly value both upward mobility and fairness, so there is genuine disagreement about which economic approach best serves those ideals.

## Important qualifications

- **Republicans are not uniform.** There are libertarian, religious-conservative, establishment, populist, and moderate wings of the party.  
- **Democrats also do not represent all American values perfectly.** They may be stronger on inclusion, social protections, and institutional norms, but can be criticized for bureaucratic expansion, elite cultural attitudes, or policies some see as restrictive of economic or religious freedom.  
- **Public opinion is not the only measure of values.** A position can be morally important even if it is not currently supported by a majority.

## Bottom line

There is credible evidence that Republicans strongly represent American values of individualism, religious liberty, entrepreneurship, patriotism, local control, and skepticism of centralized power. However, the claim becomes much weaker if “American values” centrally include pluralism, equal civil rights, majority support on key social issues, and an unwavering commitment to democratic institutions and election legitimacy.

So the most defensible conclusion is not that Republicans simply represent American values *better*, but that they represent one powerful and enduring interpretation of those values—while Democrats represent another.

Whether Republicans “better represent American values” depends heavily on which values are emphasized. Americans do not share one fixed political value set: many combine conservative views on some issues with liberal or moderate views on others.

## Evidence supporting the claim

### 1. Strong alignment with values of tradition, religion, and patriotism
Republicans are more likely to foreground values that many Americans regard as central to national identity:

- Religious faith and religious liberty
- Family formation and parental authority
- Respect for the military, police, and national symbols
- Individual responsibility and self-reliance
- Skepticism of rapid cultural change

The United States remains more religious than many comparable wealthy democracies, and large parts of the country—especially rural areas, the South, and many small towns—hold socially conservative views. Republican messaging often speaks directly to those constituencies.

### 2. Individual liberty and limited government have broad appeal
Core Republican ideas such as lower taxes, entrepreneurship, property rights, and suspicion of excessive government power draw on longstanding American traditions. The country’s political culture has historically included a strong preference for individual initiative and wariness of centralized authority.

Even voters who favor government programs often dislike perceived waste, bureaucracy, or high taxes. Republican arguments about fiscal restraint and economic freedom therefore resonate beyond committed conservatives.

### 3. Public concern about crime, immigration, and disorder can favor Republicans
Republicans often perform well when voters prioritize:

- Border enforcement and immigration control
- Public safety and crime reduction
- Inflation, government spending, and economic uncertainty
- Opposition to elite institutions or political correctness

Polls frequently show that many Americans, including some independents and Democrats, want stronger border enforcement and are uneasy about rapid social or demographic change. Republican rhetoric can capture those concerns more directly than Democratic rhetoric.

### 4. Republicans represent a large and durable section of the electorate
The Republican Party regularly wins national elections, controls many state governments, and has deep support across wide geographic areas. That alone is evidence that its values are authentically American for tens of millions of people. A party that repeatedly earns roughly half of votes in competitive elections cannot reasonably be described as outside the American mainstream.

## Evidence against the claim

### 1. On many specific issues, national majorities favor positions closer to Democrats
When values are measured through individual policy questions rather than partisan identity, Republicans often hold positions that are less popular nationally. Examples commonly include:

- Legal access to abortion in at least some circumstances
- Same-sex marriage and legal protections for LGBTQ people
- Stronger environmental and climate policies
- Universal or expanded health-care coverage
- More restrictive gun laws, such as background checks
- A path to legal status or citizenship for many undocumented immigrants already in the country

The details matter: Americans may favor border security while also supporting legal status for long-term undocumented residents, or favor some abortion restrictions while opposing near-total bans. Republican platforms do not always reflect those mixed majoritarian views.

### 2. America is increasingly diverse and socially pluralistic
The country is racially, religiously, and culturally diverse, and younger Americans in particular are generally more accepting of racial diversity, LGBTQ rights, gender equality, and secular public life than older generations.

Republican appeals to a traditional cultural order can feel representative to some Americans but exclusionary to others—especially immigrants, religious minorities, racial minorities, LGBTQ Americans, and voters who see pluralism as a central American value.

### 3. Democratic values are also deeply American
Values often associated with Democrats—equal opportunity, civil rights, social insurance, labor protections, public education, and protection for marginalized groups—also have strong roots in American history. The New Deal, civil-rights movement, women’s-rights movement, and expansion of voting rights are all part of the national story.

If “American values” means equality before the law, social mobility, democratic inclusion, and a government capable of addressing collective problems, Democrats may appear at least as representative as Republicans.

### 4. Concerns about democracy and constitutional norms
A major objection is that some Republican leaders and voters have supported claims or actions that critics view as undermining election administration, trust in elections, peaceful transfer of power, or institutional checks and balances.

Because commitment to constitutional democracy is widely considered a core American value, Republican association with election denialism or efforts to overturn election outcomes damages the case that the party better represents national values. At the same time, Republicans argue that election integrity concerns are legitimate and that criticism of institutions is not inherently anti-democratic; the dispute turns on evidence and on whether challenges respect lawful processes.

### 5. Electoral success is not identical to majority representation
Republicans can exercise substantial power while receiving fewer total votes nationally because of the Electoral College, Senate representation, districting, and geographic concentration of voters. Those institutions are constitutional, but they mean party control does not necessarily prove that a party represents a national majority’s preferences.

## Overall assessment

The strongest case for Republicans is that they represent enduring American values of religious faith, national identity, self-reliance, order, local control, economic freedom, and skepticism of government. Those values are real, widespread, and especially powerful in many regions.

The strongest case against the claim is that the nation’s overall electorate often supports more socially liberal and economically interventionist policies than the Republican Party does, while many Americans see pluralism, civil rights, environmental protection, and democratic norms as equally fundamental American values.

So the most defensible conclusion is not that Republicans simply do or do not represent American values. They represent one major, historically rooted interpretation of them—often called conservative, traditionalist, or populist—but not the whole of a highly diverse country.

## Evidence supporting the claim

**1. Greater alignment with pluralism and demographic diversity**  
Democrats generally emphasize racial, religious, gender, and sexual-orientation inclusion; immigration; and protections for minority groups. Those positions can be seen as reflecting an increasingly diverse United States. Democrats also tend to receive strong support from racial and ethnic minorities, younger voters, many urban residents, and religiously unaffiliated Americans.

The party’s support for public education, health coverage, labor protections, Social Security, voting access, and anti-discrimination law reflects a view that American equality requires more than formal legal rights. This draws on traditions associated with the New Deal, civil-rights movement, and “equal opportunity” ideal.

**3. Defense of civil rights and democratic participation**  
Democrats often advocate expanded voting access, protections against discrimination, reproductive autonomy, and separation of church and state. Supporters argue these positions fit core constitutional values of equal citizenship, individual liberty, and representative democracy.

**4. Public opinion often favors particular Democratic policy goals**  
Even when voters do not identify as Democrats, many individual Democratic-leaning policies—such as protecting Social Security and Medicare, regulating prescription-drug costs, maintaining abortion access in at least some circumstances, and requiring background checks for gun purchases—have frequently received majority support in national polling. That suggests parts of the Democratic agenda align with widely held preferences.

**5. Acceptance of government as a tool for collective problems**  
Many Americans expect government to respond to economic insecurity, disasters, public health threats, infrastructure needs, and environmental risks. Democratic policy tends to take this expectation seriously, which supporters regard as a practical expression of mutual responsibility.

## Evidence against the claim

**1. Many Americans prioritize limited government and self-reliance**  
A major American political tradition emphasizes low taxes, local control, private enterprise, religious faith, gun rights, and skepticism of federal power. Republicans tend to represent these views more directly. Democrats’ support for regulation, taxation, and expansive federal programs can therefore conflict with deeply rooted American values of individual liberty and limited government.

**2. Cultural liberalism is not universally representative**  
Democratic positions on abortion, gender identity, religion in public life, immigration, policing, and family norms can alienate socially conservative Americans. The United States remains substantially religious and includes many voters who see traditional family structures, religious liberty, and abortion restrictions as moral commitments rather than merely political preferences.

**3. Electoral support does not show a clear nationwide Democratic consensus**  
Democrats have won many national popular votes in recent decades, especially in presidential elections, but the country is closely divided. Republicans regularly win the presidency, Congress, governorships, and state legislatures. A party that represents “American values” broadly would presumably enjoy more decisive and consistent majorities than either party has.

**4. Democratic constituencies are not the whole country**  
Democrats are strongest in large metropolitan areas and among college-educated, younger, and minority voters. Republicans are stronger among rural voters, many working-class White voters, evangelical Christians, and many small-town communities. Treating one coalition as uniquely American risks implying that the other coalition is less legitimately American.

**5. Critics see tensions between Democratic policies and some civic values**  
Opponents argue that some Democratic approaches can undermine freedom of speech, parental authority, public safety, fiscal restraint, or national cohesion. Whether those criticisms are fair varies by issue, but they reflect real disagreements over what liberty and equality require in practice.

## The key complication: “American values” are plural

The strongest conclusion is not that Democrats clearly do or do not represent American values. Rather, Democrats represent one major and legitimate American tradition:

- **egalitarianism**
- **pluralism**
- **civil-rights protections**
- **collective responsibility**
- **an active federal government**

Republicans represent another:

- **limited government**
- **individual responsibility**
- **religious and cultural traditionalism**
- **localism**
- **market-oriented freedom**

Both traditions have deep roots in American history and substantial public support. Democrats may better reflect Americans who prioritize inclusion, social insurance, and government action to widen opportunity. They do not clearly represent Americans better overall, because the electorate remains closely divided and because American values themselves are contested.

Americans broadly endorse ideals that can point in different political directions: liberty and equality, individual responsibility and social protection, religious freedom and pluralism, patriotism and dissent, limited government and effective public institutions.

## Evidence supporting the claim

**1. Strong alignment with individualism and self-reliance**  
Republicans generally emphasize personal responsibility, entrepreneurship, work, private charity, and skepticism of government dependence. Those themes have deep roots in American political culture and appeal especially to voters who see the country as built on independence and opportunity.

**2. Support for free enterprise and property rights**  
The party traditionally favors lower taxes, deregulation, private-sector solutions, and protections for property owners and businesses. Since market capitalism is central to the U.S. economic system, this is a significant claim to representing a longstanding American tradition.

**3. Religious and family-oriented values**  
Republicans tend to receive strong support from white evangelical Christians, many Catholics, and socially conservative voters. Their positions on abortion, religious liberty, parental authority, and traditional family structures resonate with Americans who see faith and family as the foundation of public morality.

**4. Patriotism, national sovereignty, and law-and-order**  
Republican rhetoric often stresses the flag, military strength, border enforcement, policing, and national sovereignty. These are values with broad public support, especially during periods of insecurity or rapid social change.

**5. Electoral evidence**  
Republicans have repeatedly won national elections, govern many states, and remain highly competitive even when they lose the national popular vote. That demonstrates that their message reflects the values of a very large share of Americans, particularly in rural areas, the South, and many working-class communities.

## Evidence against the claim

**1. American values include equality and pluralism as well as individualism**  
The country’s foundational ideals also include equal protection, civil rights, religious diversity, immigration, and political inclusion. Republicans’ positions on voting rules, immigration enforcement, LGBTQ rights, abortion restrictions, and affirmative action can be seen by critics as placing traditional social norms or majority preferences above equal inclusion and personal autonomy.

**2. Tension between “limited government” and social-policy enforcement**  
Republicans often argue for less government intervention in economic life, but many support substantial state power in areas such as abortion regulation, school curriculum, immigration enforcement, drug policy, and gender-related issues. Critics see this as inconsistent with a broad principle of limited government and individual liberty.

**3. Fiscal record complicates claims of small government**  
While Republicans campaign on fiscal restraint, Republican administrations and Congresses have at times increased federal deficits and debt, including through tax cuts without corresponding spending reductions, military spending, and emergency measures. This weakens the argument that the party consistently represents fiscal conservatism.

**4. Tension with free-market principles**  
Recent Republican politics has included support for tariffs, industrial policy, restrictions on foreign investment or trade, and pressure on corporations over cultural issues. Supporters call this economic nationalism; critics argue it departs from traditional American commitments to open markets and limited government intervention.

**5. Democratic norms and institutional trust**  
A major test is commitment to constitutional democracy: acceptance of election outcomes, peaceful transfers of power, an independent judiciary, free press, and constraints on executive authority. Republican officials and voters vary substantially on these questions, but efforts to challenge the 2020 election result and the January 6 attack created serious evidence against the claim that the party consistently embodies constitutional-democratic values. At the same time, many Republican officeholders rejected attempts to overturn results and defended election administration.

**6. Representation is broader than winning elections**  
The Republican coalition is strong but not demographically representative of every part of the country. It is generally older, more rural, more religious, and whiter than the country overall, though it has made gains among some Latino, Black, Asian American, and working-class voters. Democrats more often win support from younger voters, racial and ethnic minorities, urban voters, secular Americans, and many college-educated voters. No party fully represents the whole population.

## A fair conclusion

Republicans plausibly represent an important set of American values: self-reliance, private enterprise, religious commitment, patriotism, community order, and skepticism of centralized power. For Americans who prioritize those values, the answer may be yes.

But they do not clearly represent American values *better overall*, because equally American values—pluralism, racial and gender equality, civil liberties, democratic accountability, immigration, social mobility, and public provision for shared needs—often point toward different policies and are strongly represented by Democrats or by neither party consistently.

The strongest evidence-based conclusion is that Republicans represent **one major and historically rooted American value tradition**, rather than a uniquely authoritative version of “American values.”

When Mara first saw the red hats, they were piled beside the cash register at the gas station off Route 9.

The station had once sold fishing lures, lottery tickets, and dusty maps of the county. Now it sold those things too, but the hats occupied the most prominent shelf: bright red, block letters, impossible to ignore.

MAKE AMERICA GREAT AGAIN.

Mara stood in line holding a coffee she did not want. She had driven three hours from the city to clear out her father’s house after his stroke, and the gas station was the first place she had stopped since crossing the county line.

Behind the counter, a teenager with a lip ring scanned her coffee.

“Passing through?” he asked.

“Sort of.”

He nodded toward the hats. “People buy those like candy.”

Mara looked at them. “Do they?”

“Depends who you ask.”

That answer followed her all the way to her father’s house.

It was a narrow white farmhouse at the edge of a field gone wild with autumn weeds. Her father had lived there alone since her mother died, stubbornly refusing offers to move closer to Mara or into a smaller place. The porch sagged. Wind chimes made from old utensils clicked in the breeze.

Inside, there were stacks of newspapers, prescription bottles, and framed photographs of Mara at every age: gap-toothed, angry-faced, graduation-gowned, holding her newborn daughter.

There was also a red hat on the kitchen table.

Mara stopped at the doorway.

Her father, Eli, sat in his recliner by the window, thinner than she remembered, a blanket over his knees. The television was muted. On the screen, a crowd waved flags beneath a giant flag.

“You wearing that now?” she asked.

He glanced toward the table. “Sometimes.”

Mara put down her bag more sharply than she intended. “Dad.”

“What?”

“You know what that means to me.”

He studied her for a moment. “I know what you think it means.”

“That’s not the same thing?”

“No,” he said quietly. “It isn’t.”

Mara wanted to argue immediately. She wanted to list every rally clip she had watched late at night, every chant that made her stomach tighten, every story about threats, scapegoats, and people who seemed to confuse cruelty with courage. To her, MAGA had become more than a campaign slogan. It was a warning siren. It was nationalism stripped of its old caution signs: a promise that the country could be restored only by deciding who belonged and who did not.

But her father looked tired, and the room smelled faintly of soup and dust.

So she said, “Why?”

He looked back at the muted television.

“Because I’m scared,” he said.

The simplicity of it disarmed her.

“Of what?”

“Of being forgotten.” He tapped a knuckle against the armrest. “This town had a factory. Your grandfather worked there. I worked there. Half the people on this road worked there. Then it closed, and everybody said we should retrain, move, adapt. Like it was that easy.”

Mara sat across from him.

“Some people did leave,” he continued. “Some people got sick. Some people started drinking too much. And the politicians came around during elections and told us we mattered. Then they left again.”

“And MAGA makes you feel like you matter?”

Her father gave a small, embarrassed shrug. “Sometimes.”

Mara looked at the hat on the table. Its red seemed too loud for the faded kitchen.

“I understand wanting that,” she said. “I do. But Dad, that movement doesn’t just say people like you have been ignored. It says other people are the reason. Immigrants. Muslims. Black people. Gay people. Anyone who doesn’t fit some picture of a ‘real American.’”

“I don’t believe that.”

“Maybe you don’t. But plenty of people do.”

Eli’s expression tightened. “You think I’m one of them?”

“I think you’re helping them.”

The sentence hung between them.

Outside, a truck passed on the county road, its tires hissing over wet pavement.

Her father turned toward the window. “Your mother would’ve told you not to say something like that.”

“Mom would’ve told you not to wear the hat.”

That almost made him laugh. Almost.

For the next several days, Mara sorted through the house. She filled boxes with old records, winter coats, tools that no longer had a purpose. Each afternoon, she drove into town for groceries or paperwork. And everywhere she went, the red hats appeared: on a man pumping gas, on a bumper sticker beside an American flag, on a woman in the pharmacy buying cough medicine.

At first, the hats made Mara furious. They felt like declarations. Like each one said: There is an America you are trying to ruin, and we are here to take it back.

But as the week went on, she began to notice the people beneath them.

There was the mechanic who fixed her father’s truck and refused payment because Eli had once helped him after a flood. There was the old woman at the diner who wore a hat but also kept a jar by the register for a local family whose house had burned down. There was the teenage cashier at the gas station, who told Mara he hated politics but wore a red cap at work because his manager said it helped sales.

None of that changed what Mara believed.

If anything, it made her belief more complicated and more urgent.

Dangerous nationalism, she realized, did not always arrive looking like a villain. It could arrive carrying a casserole. It could be worn by someone who loved his grandchildren. It could grow in the soil of real pain: abandoned towns, lost jobs, wounded pride, fear of being invisible.

That did not make it harmless.

It made it harder to fight.

One evening, Mara found her father in the garage, standing beside an old metal cabinet. He was wearing the red hat.

She froze.

He had a box in his hands. On the side, written in black marker, were the words UNION PAPERS.

“I didn’t know you still had those,” she said.

“Didn’t know I did either.”

Mara took the photograph.

“Look at that,” she said.

“What?”

“You fought together.”

“We had to.”

“And now you’re wearing a symbol tied to people who want everyone to be afraid of each other.”

Her father sighed. “You make everything sound so simple.”

“No,” Mara said. “I think they make it sound simple. That’s the problem.”

She held up the photograph.

“They tell you the country was stolen from you,” she said. “They tell you the answer is to take it back from somebody else. But this—” She tapped the picture. “This was America too. People who didn’t agree about everything, but knew they needed each other.”

Her father’s eyes moved from the photograph to the hat on his head

When Daniel Mercer hung the flag outside his hardware store every morning, he did it before he unlocked the doors.

The flag had belonged to his father, a Vietnam veteran who had kept it folded in a cedar chest until Daniel’s mother died. It was not a fancy flag. The edges were worn, one corner had been stitched by hand, and the blue field had faded a little under years of sun. But Daniel raised it carefully, using the same brass clips his father had used.

“Morning, Dan,” called Mrs. Alvarez from across the street, carrying a paper bag of pastries from her bakery.

“Morning,” Daniel replied. “Smells like you’re trying to ruin my diet.”

“You don’t have a diet,” she said.

“That’s true.”

The town of Cedar Ridge sat between cornfields and a wide river in western Ohio. It had once been a factory town, back when the mill made tractor parts and the train depot ran freight day and night. Now the mill was a warehouse for an online retailer, and the depot had been converted into a craft brewery with string lights over the patio.

Daniel had watched the town change slowly, then all at once.

His son had moved to Texas after college because there was no work nearby. His daughter, Emily, lived outside Columbus and worked in a hospital. The old VFW hall had fewer men every year. The diner on Main Street had replaced its local newspaper rack with a shelf of charging stations.

Daniel did not begrudge young people their futures. But sometimes he felt that the country he had been taught to love—hard work, family, faith, neighbors looking after one another—was being treated like an embarrassing relic.

That was why, four years earlier, he had put a red hat behind the counter.

MAKE AMERICA GREAT AGAIN.

At first, it had been a joke from his brother-in-law. Then customers began asking whether he had more. Daniel ordered a box. Before long, he had hats, bumper stickers, and shirts stacked beside the register.

To Daniel, MAGA was not about hating anyone. He told people that whenever they asked.

“It means remembering what made this place work,” he would say. “It means that ordinary people shouldn’t be ignored by folks in big offices who’ve never fixed a fence, served in uniform, or worried about making payroll.”

Some agreed. Some rolled their eyes. A few stopped coming to the store.

Daniel hated that part.

He did not enjoy arguments. He had spent most of his adult life repairing leaking pipes, replacing broken windowpanes, and helping people find the right screw for a cabinet hinge. He liked problems with clear solutions.

But politics had become personal in Cedar Ridge.

One Saturday, a week before Independence Day, Daniel was unloading bags of potting soil when Emily pulled into the lot with her two children in the back seat.

“Grandpa!” shouted seven-year-old Noah, launching himself from the car before Emily could finish parking.

Daniel scooped him up. “There’s my little outlaw.”

“I’m not an outlaw,” Noah protested. “I’m a scientist.”

“Even better.”

Emily hugged him, then glanced toward the display near the register through the front window.

“You’re still selling those?” she asked.

Daniel set Noah down. “I am.”

“Dad.”

“What?”

She sighed. “Nothing. I just wish you understood how it looks.”

He leaned against the tailgate of his truck. “How does it look?”

“Like you support everything people say under that banner.”

“I support loving your country.”

“So does everyone else.”

“Not everyone means it the same way.”

Emily folded her arms. She had inherited his stubbornness, though she would never admit it.

“Maybe that’s the problem,” she said. “Everybody thinks they own patriotism.”

Daniel wanted to answer quickly. He felt the familiar heat rise in his chest. But Noah had found a plastic watering can and was filling it with gravel from the edge of the lot, so Daniel took a breath.

“What does patriotism mean to you?” he asked.

Emily looked surprised.

“It means trying to make the country better,” she said after a moment. “Even when that means admitting it’s done things wrong.”

Daniel nodded slowly.

“That’s fair,” he said.

“And what does it mean to you?”

He looked at the flag moving above the storefront. It snapped once in the warm wind.

“It means not being ashamed of it,” he said. “It means remembering the people who built it, fought for it, and kept it going when nobody was watching. It means believing we don’t have to apologize for wanting strong borders, good jobs, safe streets, and respect for the people who live here.”

Emily looked at him for a long moment.

“I know you believe that,” she said quietly. “I just don’t think everyone wearing those hats believes it for the same reasons.”

Daniel had no easy reply to that.

That evening, Cedar Ridge held its annual Independence Day parade. Kids decorated bicycles with red, white, and blue streamers. The high school band marched slightly out of time. Veterans rode in antique convertibles, waving at crowds gathered beneath the maple trees.

Daniel stood near the courthouse in a blue work shirt, his old MAGA hat on his head. Beside him stood Mrs. Alvarez, holding a small American flag in one hand and a bakery box in the other.

“You know,” she said, “your daughter’s probably right about one thing.”

“Only one?” Daniel asked.

“She is right often enough to be annoying.”

He smiled.

Mrs. Alvarez watched the parade pass. “Patriotism is complicated. My father became a citizen when he was forty-three. He cried at the ceremony. He loved this country more fiercely than anyone I’ve ever known. But he also complained about it every day.”

Daniel laughed. “Sounds American.”

“Exactly.”

A group of children came down the street carrying a banner that read CEDAR RIDGE YOUTH BASEBALL. Behind them walked the volunteer firefighters, then the local nurses’ association. Emily was among them in blue scrubs, waving when she saw him. Noah marched beside her, proudly holding a hand-painted sign that said THANK YOU FIRST RESPONDERS.

Daniel lifted his hat.

For a moment, he felt something loosen inside him. He had spent so much time fearing that America was disappearing that he had overlooked the pieces of it still standing all around him: the nurse caring for strangers through long nights, the immigrant baker handing out free cookies to firefighters, the teenage boy playing “America the Beautiful” badly but sincerely on a trumpet, the old veterans waving from their cars.

Daniel still believed MAGA represented authentic patriotism. To him, it was a declaration that America’s traditions, workers, families, and sovereignty mattered—that the people who loved their towns and flew their flags should not be dismissed as backward or forgotten.

But as the parade moved on, he understood something else.

The country was bigger than any hat, any slogan, any election.

Patriotism, he thought, was not proven by who shouted loudest. It was proven by who showed up—at the hospital, at the fire station, at the voting booth, at the neighbor’s door after a storm.

Mrs. Alvarez handed him a cookie shaped like a star.

“You going to share that?” she asked.

Daniel broke it in half and handed a piece to Noah, who had run over from the parade route.

Mara had signed up to help furnish apartments and teach English.

Her mother had called it “kindness with paperwork.”

Her brother, Evan, had called it “naïve.”

Mara had not spoken to him in three weeks.

“Your brother’s over there,” said a voice beside her.

It was Mr. Alvarez, who owned the bakery downtown. He held a thermos in one hand and wore a wool cap dusted with flour, as if he had come straight from kneading dough.

Her grandfather had looked out the window for a long time.

“So did you.”

Someone across the street shouted, “Go home!”

The little girl pressed closer to her mother.

Evan turned toward the voice. Mara watched his face. He did not cheer. He did not smile. He just stood there, silent, the red hat bright against the gray day.

“That,” Mara said, “is what I mean.”

The man shouted again. Others joined him, though not everyone. The sound became a rough, ugly wave.

Evan looked at the mother and child. Then at the courthouse flag overhead, snapping hard in the wind.

“Our grandfather would hate this,” Mara said.

“He voted Republican.”

“That isn’t what I said.”

For the first time, Evan’s anger broke. Not vanished, exactly—anger like his rarely vanished—but cracked enough to let something else show through.

“I just want things to be better,” he said.

“So do I.”

“They keep saying nobody listens to us.”

“Maybe nobody did,” Mara said. “But listening doesn’t mean agreeing that someone else has to be pushed out.”

The chant faltered as police moved to separate the groups. Mr. Alvarez stepped beside Mara, not speaking. On the other side of the street, several people lowered their signs. Others raised them higher.

Evan reached up and removed his hat.

He held it in both hands, turning it over once.

“I don’t agree with you,” he said.

“I know.”

“But I don’t want that little girl scared of me.”

Mara nodded. “Then don’t be someone she has to fear.”

He looked toward the courthouse again. The girl had noticed a patch of dirty snow beside the steps and was trying to kick it with the toe of her boot. Her mother was speaking to a volunteer, who pointed toward a van waiting at the curb.

Evan exhaled.

Then he crossed the street—not to rejoin the chanting crowd, but to stand at its edge.

He did not make a speech. He did not apologize. He simply told the man with the bullhorn to stop shouting at children.

The man laughed at him. Called him weak. Called him a traitor.

Evan’s shoulders stiffened, but he did not put the hat back on.

Mara watched from the sidewalk, her sign trembling in her cold hands.

When Eli Mercer hung the flag outside his hardware store every morning, he did it before he turned on the lights.

The flag was old, its colors softened by rain and sun, its brass grommets polished by his thumb whenever he took it down at night. His father had flown it before him, above the same narrow storefront on Main Street, back when the store sold feed, nails, and kerosene lamps. Eli had inherited the building, the business, and a particular understanding of what it meant to love a country: you worked, you paid what you owed, you looked after your neighbors, and you never forgot the people who had built the place before you.

By 2024, a red cap sat beside the cash register.

MAKE AMERICA GREAT AGAIN, it said in white letters.

Some customers nodded approvingly when they saw it. Others frowned. A few avoided looking at it altogether.

Eli didn’t care much for arguments in the store. He had learned that arguments rarely ended with anyone changing their mind, and he needed to sell pipe fittings to Republicans and Democrats alike. But when people asked, he answered plainly.

“MAGA’s patriotism,” he would say, measuring out bolts into a brown paper bag. “It means we ought to be proud of this country instead of apologizing for it all the time.”

Most often, that ended the conversation.

One wet Tuesday in October, a woman named Marisol came in looking for weather stripping. She taught history at the high school and had been buying supplies from Eli for years. Her father had fixed the shop’s front awning after a storm in the nineties, and Eli always gave her a small discount, though neither of them mentioned it.

She saw the cap on the counter.

“You still wearing that?” she asked.

“Still believing it,” Eli said.

Marisol picked up a roll of foam insulation. “And what exactly do you believe?”

Eli leaned against the counter. Outside, rain threaded down the windows, blurring the empty street.

“I believe this country ought to put its own people first,” he said. “I believe we’ve forgotten that hard work matters. I believe ordinary folks get talked down to by people who’ve never had dirt under their nails. And I believe patriotism means wanting America to be strong enough to protect the people who live here.”

Marisol nodded slowly. “That sounds like patriotism.”

“It is patriotism.”

“But is it only patriotism if someone agrees with your version of America?”

Eli’s face tightened. “I didn’t say that.”

“No,” she said gently. “You didn’t.”

She paid for the weather stripping and left, taking the question with her but leaving its shadow behind.

That evening, Eli drove to the VFW hall for the town’s candidate forum. He went wearing his favorite work jacket and the red cap. Half the room seemed to be wearing one too. The other half sat with folded arms, clutching notepads or paper cups of weak coffee.

The candidates argued about taxes, the border, schools, factories that had closed twenty years ago and never reopened. Eli applauded when one candidate spoke about bringing jobs back home. He applauded when another promised to support veterans. He applauded loudest when a retired machinist stood up during public comments and said, “We’re tired of being told America is something to be ashamed of.”

Then a boy from the high school stepped to the microphone.

His name was Noah Patel. Eli recognized him as the quiet kid who bought model paint and small tools from the store. Noah’s father was a doctor at the clinic. His mother ran the pharmacy.

“My grandfather became a citizen last year,” Noah said, his voice shaking at first. “He came here from India after working for decades as an engineer. At his citizenship ceremony, he cried during the Pledge of Allegiance. He said America gave him the chance to belong somewhere because he was willing to work for it.”

The room grew quieter.

“My grandfather is patriotic,” Noah continued. “My mom is patriotic. My dad is patriotic. I’m patriotic. But sometimes when people say they want America back, I wonder if they mean they want people like us to feel like guests again.”

Eli looked down at the cap in his hands.

Noah finished speaking and returned to his seat. No one clapped at first. Then Marisol, sitting near the back, began to applaud. Others joined in—not everyone, but enough.

On the drive home, Eli passed the football field, where the stadium lights glowed against the rain. A banner hung over the entrance: HOME OF THE EAGLES. Beneath it, a cluster of teenagers laughed together under the awning. Black, white, Hispanic, Asian. Some wore school jackets, some hoodies, one wore a turban beneath a rain hood.

Eli remembered being sixteen, standing in that same parking lot with his father after a game. His father had pointed toward the field and said, “This is what the country is, son. Not perfect. Never has been. But it belongs to whoever is willing to help carry it.”

At the time, Eli had thought he understood.

The next morning, he unlocked the hardware store before sunrise. The street was still dark, and the town was quiet except for a delivery truck groaning somewhere near the diner.

He carried the flag outside and fastened it to its pole. It lifted in the cold breeze, red and white and blue against a pale gray sky.

Then he went inside, set the red cap back beside the register, and stood looking at it for a long moment.

He still believed America needed strong borders. He still believed its workers deserved better than empty promises and shuttered factories. He still believed people had been too quick to mock the places and traditions that had held towns like his together.

And he still believed MAGA represented authentic American patriotism—not because it was flawless, not because everyone who wore the hat was right, but because, to him, it named a longing he understood: for dignity, self-government, security, and pride in a country worth defending.

But he also knew patriotism could not be merely a demand that the nation look backward.

It had to be a promise.

When Marisol came in later that afternoon, Eli was helping Noah Patel choose a set of screwdrivers for a robotics project. Noah was explaining, with great seriousness, why precision tools mattered more than size.

Marisol watched from the end of the aisle.

Eli rang up Noah’s purchase and handed him the bag.

“Good luck with the project,” he said.

“Thanks, Mr. Mercer.”

After Noah left, Marisol placed a box of lightbulbs on the counter.

“You hear him?” Eli asked.

“Hear who?”

“The kid. He’s building something.”

Marisol smiled. “That’s generally what robotics is.”

Eli looked out the window at the flag over the storefront.

“I reckon that’s the job,” he said. “Building something. Keeping what’s good. Making room for the people willing to help.”

Marisol studied him, then glanced at the red cap beside the register.

“That sounds like patriotism too,” she said.

Eli nodded.

“It is.”
